name: Yaya Bey
label: Big Dada
lede: A rapper's daughter who was told not to sing, four self-released records in, and then a No. 9 finish on Pitchfork's 2022 list.

eras.title: A rapper's daughter starts writing
eras.text: Yaya Bey grew up in New York with a father on the Juice Crew's fringes and started writing songs as a kid. Her first three albums came out on Elevated while she worked day jobs, changed cities and went through a divorce.

years.src: Yaya Bey (Wikipedia) · Grand Daddy I.U. (Wikipedia) · Permanent Rotation
years.h: Hidaiyah Bey is born in Queens, daughter of a Cold Chillin' rapper
years.p: Wikipedia gives her birth date as August 4, 1990 and names her father as [[Grand Daddy I.U.|f807e647-ee9a-4b57-9729-250e13a28984]], the suit-and-tie Juice Crew rapper.
years.xp:
Her father, Ayub Bey, signed to Cold Chillin' Records in 1989 after [[Biz Markie|48b48175-5ffd-49a2-88e2-ca84118544ca]] heard his demo, and his debut Smooth Assassin came out in 1990, according to Wikipedia.

The Vinyl Factory reports he told her she could not and should not sing, but encouraged her to write songs. She started writing poetry and songs in elementary school and found a Roberta Flack and Donny Hathaway record in her grandmother's basement around age 13.

years.src: In Conversation: Yaya Bey · Yaya Bey (Wikipedia)
years.h: The Many Alter-Egos of Trill'eta Brown, her first album
years.p: Self-styled and released on Elevated, it is where she first gets the name Yaya Bey out into the world.
years.xp: Clash lists it as her first project. It came four years before anyone outside her circle was paying attention.

years.src: In Conversation: Yaya Bey · Yaya Bey (Wikipedia)
years.p: The second Elevated album. Bey told Clash it was made while her marriage was ending.

years.src: In Conversation: Yaya Bey · SPOTLIGHT: Yaya Bey
years.h: Bey moves from D.C. to New York, and Big Dada calls
years.p: Clash says she relocated in April 2019. The same interview says Big Dada first reached out that year, but the timing wasn't right yet.
years.xp:
Bey describes the label as giving her advice and resources and letting her do what she feels she needs to do. They would sign her two years later.

Sources differ on the details of her early years: Wikipedia and The Luna Collective place her birth and upbringing in Queens, while Clash notes her earlier stretch living in D.C.

eras.title: Madison Tapes and Big Dada
eras.text: Madison Tapes is where Bey finds the sound people now call hers, and Big Dada relaunches her with an EP. It is the start of her run of critical attention.

years.src: In Conversation: Yaya Bey · Interview: Yaya Bey Came Here to Live
years.h: Madison Tapes is the record that finds her sound
years.p: Released on Elevated; Bey told Clash it was where she found her authentic sound, and Range calls it her breakthrough.
years.xp: Wikipedia dates the start of her professional music career to this album (she had already released three albums on Elevated), which is how the press usually tells it.

years.src: In Conversation: Yaya Bey · Yaya Bey (Wikipedia)
years.h: The Things I Can't Take with Me is her first Big Dada release
years.p: The EP is the label's relaunch of Bey after two years of conversations, and it was reviewed by Pitchfork, Rolling Stone and The Guardian.

eras.title: North Star
eras.text: Her Big Dada debut album lands in June and ends the year at No. 9 on Pitchfork's list. By December her father is gone.

years.cap: Remember Your North Star, Big Dada, 2022
q: The whole concept of a North Star just feels more sure of itself.
years.src: Yaya Bey announces new album · Yaya Bey - Remember Your North Star · Permanent Rotation
years.h: Remember Your North Star: Pitchfork gives it 8.6, No. 9 of 2022
years.p: An 18-track album opened by "Keisha", co-produced by Bey with [[Aja Grant|75f15961-340a-4619-9c4a-0002469fb729]] of Phony Ppl and [[DJ Nativesun|b4efd9e0-6754-45a0-8f82-99f7575d54ce]]. Pitchfork gave it 8.6 and ranked it No. 9 of the year.
years.xp:
Album of the Year lists it at No. 9 on Pitchfork's 50 Best Albums of 2022, No. 14 at BrooklynVegan and No. 32 at The Guardian, with Pitchfork's 86 the highest of its four critic scores there.

Bey called the record her thesis: in her words to BrooklynVegan, we do want love of self and love from our community. The Vinyl Factory quotes Pitchfork's Eric Torres on how it braids confidence and vulnerability.

years.h: It was going to be called Safe Travels
years.p: Bey changed the title of Remember Your North Star because the new one felt more self-assured, she told The Vinyl Factory.
Wikipedia gives the date and his age; it does not state a cause. He would appear on his daughter's next album.

eras.title: Ten Fold, then a new label
eras.text: She follows the breakthrough with an EP, a grief-heavy album for Big Dada, and then two records on Drink Sum Wtr. The work keeps getting warmer and the attention stays.

years.p: A Big Dada EP released the year after the album, per Wikipedia's discography.

q: I don't want to be my work. I want time to really be present.
years.src: Ten Fold (Wikipedia) · Interview: Yaya Bey Came Here to Live
years.h: Ten Fold: Pitchfork 8.4 and Best New Music
years.p: Sixteen tracks in 39 minutes, with her late father and producer [[Exaktly|d2d25ef3-32c2-4770-93fa-cc698a8871c9]] on the record. Metacritic lists it at 89 across seven reviews.
years.xp:
Wikipedia reports that Pitchfork rated it 8.4 and named it Best New Music, and that the record is her first without a single thematic story. Reviews reference her processing her father's death across it.

In Range, she talks about not wanting to be consumed by the job of being an artist.

years.src: Yaya Bey: do it afraid review · Yaya Bey (Wikipedia)
years.h: Do It Afraid, her first for Drink Sum Wtr
years.p: Released June 20, 2025. The Line of Best Fit's John Amen gave it 8/10, calling it an ode to love.

years.h: Fidelity comes with an essay and a short film
years.p: Lead single "Blue", second single "Egyptian Musk" with NESTA; the film, "Cheers to our Fidelity", was shown at Hannah Traore Gallery in New York.
years.xp: The Luna Collective reports the project is framed around three deaths: personal, communal and the loss of innocence. It also reports that she left Brooklyn and settled in D.C. because of gentrification.
